The '''1914 German football championship''', the 12th edition of the competition, was won by [[SpVgg Fürth]], defeating [[VfB Leipzig]] 3–2 after extra time in the final. It was the last edition of the championship before the [[First World War]], with the next edition not held until after the war in 1920.<ref name="Rsssf" >{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesd/duithistpre45.html |title=German championship 1914 |date= |website= Rsssf.com |publisher= |access-date= 8 January 2016}}</ref>

For SpVgg Fürth it was the first national championship won with two more to follow in 1926 and 1929 as well as a losing appearance in the 1920 final. VfB Leipzig, the first-ever German champions in 1903, had also won the 1906 and 1913 editions as well as making a losing appearance in 1911 and was the most successful club in the pre–First World War era of the competition.<ref name="List" >{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/tablesd/duitchamp.html |title=(West) Germany -List of champions |date= |website= Rsssf.com |publisher= |access-date= 8 January 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.weltfussball.de/teams/1-fc-lok-leipzig/1/ |title= 1. FC Lok Leipzig » Steckbrief |date= |website= Weltfussball.de |publisher= |access-date= 8 January 2016|language=German|trans-title= 1. FC Lok Leipzig honours}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.weltfussball.de/teams/spvgg-greuther-fuerth/1/ |title= SpVgg Greuther Fürth » Steckbrief |date= |website= Weltfussball.de |publisher= |access-date= 8 January 2016|language=German|trans-title=SpVgg Greuther Fürth honours}}</ref>

Fürth's Karl Franz was the top scorer of the 1914 championship with five goals.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.weltfussball.de/torschuetzenkoenige/deutsche-meisterschaft/ |title=Deutsche Meisterschaft » Torschützenkönige |date= |website= Weltfussball.de |publisher= |access-date= 8 January 2016|language=German|trans-title=German championship: Top goal scorer}}</ref>

Eight clubs qualified for the competition played in knock-out format, the champions of each of the seven regional football championships as well as the defending German champions.<ref name="Rsssf" />

==Overview==
The German championship final was contested by [[SpVgg Fürth]] and [[VfB Leipzig]] with the former winning its first national championship. The final lasted for an historic 153 minutes, until SpVgg scored the winning goal, the longest game in German football history. Fürth took an early lead and Leipzig lost a player through a broken leg just before half time, unable to bring on a substitute as substitutions were not allowed in those days. Nevertheless, Leipzig equalised in the 83rd minute, forcing extra time. Fürth once more took the lead but Leipzig equalised again four minutes later. After 120 minutes the game stood at two all and the rules stipulated that the game was to be continued in 10-minute blocks of extra time until a winner was determined. A red card for Fürth player [[Hans Schmidt (footballer, born 1893)|Hans Schmidt]] in the 138 minute put both clubs at an equal number of ten players again. The game was finally decided in the 153rd minute when Karl Franz scored the winning goal for SpVgg Fürth.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.weltfussball.de/news/_n1114348_/100-jahre-meister-das-laengste-spiel/  |title=100 Jahre Meister: Das längste Spiel |date= |website= Weltfussball.de |publisher= |access-date= 8 January 2016|language=German|trans-title=100 Years Champions: The longest game}}</ref>

===Match summary===
The final, played on 31 May 1914 at Viktoria-Platz in [[Magdeburg]], pitted defending champions [[1. FC Lokomotive Leipzig|VfB Leipzig]] against southern German champions [[SpVgg Greuther Fürth|SpVgg Fürth]], coached by Englishman [[William Townley]]. Karl Franz opened the scoring for Fürth in the 17th minute before Leipzig right half Paul Michel suffered a match-ending injury in the 42nd minute; because substitutions were not permitted in 1914, Leipzig played the remainder of the match with ten men.<ref name="br">{{cite web |url=https://www.br.de/themen/sport/inhalt/fussball/2-bundesliga/spvgg-greuther-fuerth/100-jahre-deutscher-meister-fuerth-100.html |title=Spielvereinigung Fürth: Das glorreiche Meisterschaftsteam von 1914 |website=Bayerischer Rundfunk |date=30 May 2014 |access-date=16 November 2026 |language=de}}</ref>

Despite their numerical disadvantage, Leipzig equalised through [[Eduard Pendorf]] in the 83rd minute to force extra time. Frigyes Weicz restored Fürth's lead in the 104th minute, only for Leipzig captain Curt Hesse to level the score again at 2–2 in the 108th minute. With the match still tied after 120 minutes, play continued in 10-minute [[golden goal|sudden-death]] periods. Fürth half-back [[Hans Schmidt (footballer, born 1893)|Hans Schmidt]] was sent off in the 138th minute, reducing both sides to ten players, before Karl Franz scored the decisive goal in the 153rd minute to secure Fürth's first national championship in the longest completed final in German football history.<ref name="br"/>
